name: Turla
description: Turla, tracked by Microsoft as Secret Blizzard, is one of the most technically sophisticated and patient cyber-espionage units linked to Russia's FSB Center 16. Across 2025-2026 the group has continued its hallmark 'turncoat' tradecraft of hijacking other threat actors' infrastructure and malware — most notably riding on the Pakistan-linked Storm-0156 cluster's footholds in Afghan and Indian government networks to deploy its own backdoors. In mid-2025 Microsoft exposed an ISP-level adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) campaign against foreign embassies in Moscow, using captive portals and rogue 'Kaspersky AV' root certificates to deliver the ApolloShadow implant via likely SORM lawful-intercept access. In May 2026, Microsoft detailed the evolution of Turla's flagship Kazuar backdoor into a modular, leaderless peer-to-peer botnet with AMSI/ETW/WLDP bypasses — underscoring the group's continued investment in long-haul, low-noise espionage platforms targeting government, diplomatic, and defense sectors.

ttps.technique_name: Compromise Infrastructure: Network Devices / Third-Party Infrastructure
ttps.notes: Hijacks command-and-control infrastructure and footholds belonging to other threat actors (e.g. Pakistan-linked Storm-0156) to piggyback into targets
ISP-level AiTM via captive portals against foreign embassy networks in Moscow, likely leveraging SORM lawful-intercept systems

ttps.technique_name: Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
ttps.notes: ApolloShadow installs a rogue root CA disguised as Kaspersky AV to enable TLS/SSL stripping of victim traffic
Historic and ongoing use of satellite-based internet links and compromised legitimate websites/cloud services for stealthy C2
Kazuar P2P botnet supports multiple C2 channels including HTTP, WebSockets, and Exchange Web Services
Modular Kazuar 'Kernel/Bridge/Worker' architecture with leadership election ensures only one node communicates externally, minimizing exposure

ttps.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
ttps.notes: Kazuar implements AMSI, ETW, and Windows Lockdown Policy (WLDP) bypasses to evade endpoint defenses
Heavily obfuscated, modular backdoor components (Kazuar/Snake) designed for long-term undetected persistence

notable_techniques: Turncoat operations: piggybacking on rival threat actors' (Storm-0156) compromised infrastructure and tooling for its own espionage
Pioneered satellite-link hijacking for anonymous, geographically untraceable C2
ISP/telecom-level adversary-in-the-middle access against foreign embassies, likely via Russian SORM intercept systems
Rogue root certificate impersonating Kaspersky Anti-Virus to silently strip TLS from diplomatic traffic
Evolution of Kazuar into a leaderless, modular peer-to-peer botnet (Kernel/Bridge/Worker roles) for resilience
Extremely long operational lifespan (nearly 30 years) with emphasis on stealth over speed
Use of legitimate cloud and web services as low-and-slow covert channels
detection_opportunities: Audit installed root/intermediate CA certificates for unauthorized entries impersonating AV vendors (e.g. fake Kaspersky CA)
Inspect network traffic for unexpected captive-portal redirects or TLS interception on diplomatic/government endpoints operating in Russia
Hunt for backdoors or C2 callbacks originating from infrastructure previously attributed to unrelated threat actors (cross-actor infrastructure overlap)
Monitor for AMSI/ETW provider tampering or WLDP bypass indicators on endpoint security telemetry
Flag P2P-style internal host-to-host communication patterns inconsistent with normal application traffic (Kazuar Kernel/Bridge/Worker comms)
Review Exchange Web Services API usage for anomalous automated mailbox access patterns used as C2 channel
Monitor satellite/VSAT-connected network segments for unusual inbound command traffic
response_playbook: Audit installed root and intermediate CA certificates for unauthorized entries impersonating AV vendors.
Inspect for unexpected TLS interception or captive-portal redirects on diplomatic/government endpoints.
Hunt for C2 callbacks from infrastructure previously attributed to other threat actors — cross-actor infrastructure overlap is a Turla signature.
Monitor for AMSI/ETW tampering or WLDP bypass indicators.
Flag P2P-style host-to-host traffic inconsistent with normal application behavior (Kazuar Kernel/Bridge/Worker comms).
Review Exchange Web Services API usage for anomalous automated mailbox access used as a covert C2 channel.
